result: The duration of starvation determines whether flies form short-term or longer-lasting intermediate memories. Control flies starved for 16 hr formed memory lasting 2 min but not 6 or 24 hr, while 40 hr starvation improved memory performance and extended memory to 6 hr. TβhnM18 mutants starved for 16 hr showed no 2 min memory but developed memory at 6 hr lasting to 24 hr, while 40 hr starvation restored 2 min memory. The length of starvation and reinforcer strength influence appetitive memory strength.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'reveal that not only the duration of starvation matters, but it also dictates the type of memory formed, whether short- or long-term memory.' Reviewer 2 notes they 'studied how starvation modulates the establishment of short-term vs long-term memories.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the duration of starvation affects the magnitude of both short- and long-term memory.' The experimental data in Figures 1 and 2 are accepted without critique.

result: Different starvation durations produce distinct memory types with different anesthesia sensitivity profiles. Control flies at 16 hr starvation form anesthesia-sensitive intermediate memory (ITM) lasting up to 3 hr, while 40 hr starvation produces anesthesia-resistant ITM. TβhnM18 mutants at 16 hr starvation form anesthesia-sensitive LTM detectable at 24 hr, while 40 hr starvation produces anesthesia-resistant LTM and STM. Blocking dopaminergic PAM neurons immediately after training abolishes LTM in TβhnM18 mutants.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings about memory type characterization. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'illustrate that internal glycogen stores play a crucial role in this process' and that 'experiments are meticulously designed' with 'conclusions well supported by the data.' Reviewer 2 states the work 'clarified the role of the monoamine Octopamine in food-related conditioning.' The cold-shock anesthesia experiments and dopaminergic neuron blocking experiments are not questioned.

result: Octopamine acts as a negative regulator of both appetitive STM and LTM. Feeding the octopamine antagonist epinastine after training induced memory in control flies, while feeding octopamine to TβhnM18 mutants blocked LTM. Octopamine feeding before training inhibited STM. Octopamine feeding reduced sucrose intake but tyramine did not, suggesting octopamine functions as a signal for food or high internal energy levels.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'propose that octopamine serves as a negative regulator of various forms of memory' and that they 'convincingly demonstrate that octopamine negatively regulates appetitive memory formation.' Reviewer 2 notes the work shows octopamine 'is not per se involved in formation of appetitive short-term memories but rather gates memory formation by suppressing LTM when energy levels are high.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'they show that OA has a suppressive effect on learning and memory.'

result: Octopamine is not required for STM formation per se; rather, internal energy status determines whether octopamine-deficient mutants can form STM. TβhnM18 mutants form STM when energy storage is sufficiently reduced (either through prolonged starvation or glycogen reduction in both muscles and fat bodies), when using protein as reward, or in virgin vs. mated females with different energy demands. The internal energy status influences how rewards are evaluated in learning and memory.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this reinterpretation of octopamine's role. Reviewer 1 notes this 'sheds light on the enduring question of the octopaminergic neuronal system's involvement in appetitive memory formation.' Reviewer 2 states the work 'clarified the role of the monoamine Octopamine' showing it 'is not per se involved in formation of appetitive short-term memories but rather gates memory formation.' Reviewer 3 confirms this is 'an important study that extends our knowledge on OA activity in learning and memory.'

result: Internal glycogen storage in muscles and fat bodies influences memory formation and food preference. TβhnM18 mutants have higher baseline glycogen levels and reduced sucrose preference. Decreasing glycogen in muscles improved memory performance, while increasing glycogen in both muscles and fat bodies reduced memory. Low muscle glycogen after starvation positively influences STM, while high glycogen in muscles and fat body reduces STM. Glycogen levels correlate with food preferences in a sex- and mating-status-dependent manner.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these glycogen findings. Reviewer 1 states 'The authors illustrate that internal glycogen stores play a crucial role in this process, facilitated by insulin-like signaling in octopaminergic reward neurons.' Reviewer 3 notes 'they show that internal glycogen storage influences how long sucrose is remembered, and high glycogen suppresses memory.' The experimental manipulations using tissue-specific RNAi are accepted without methodological critique.

result: Insulin receptor signaling in octopaminergic reward neurons integrates internal energy status into memory formation. Activated InR is expressed in octopaminergic neuron soma. Blocking InR in octopaminergic neurons did not alter STM in control flies but restored STM in TβhnM18 mutants to normal levels. When energy levels are high, the insulin pathway suppresses STM formation and the system releases octopamine to suppress LTM formation. InR function in octopaminergic neurons regulates the rewarding properties of sucrose in STM.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this mechanism. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'propose a mechanism whereby the insulin receptor in octopaminergic neurons senses the internal energy status and subsequently modulates the activity of these neurons' and that 'The conclusions are well supported by the data.' Reviewer 2 notes the work provides 'insight about interconnections between energy levels, feeding and formation of short-term and long-term food-related memories.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'they show that insulin-like signaling in octopaminergic neurons, which is also related to internal energy storage, suppresses learning and memory.'

result: The octopaminergic reward system integrates internal energy levels into food consumption regulation via insulin receptor signaling. TβhnM18 mutants starved for 16 hr consumed less sucrose than controls, but after 40 hr starvation consumed 34% more despite still having higher glycogen levels than controls. Blocking insulin signaling in reward neurons in TβhnM18 mutants improved sucrose consumption. Increased internal energy reduces reward properties of food, resulting in decreased food consumption, but this mechanism remains intact in TβhnM18 mutants.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these food intake findings as part of the integrated story. Reviewer 1 notes the work addresses 'the interplay between internal energy homeostasis, food intake, and food-related memories' with 'solid experimental evidence.' Reviewer 2 states the authors 'systematically test the impact of internal energy levels' on behavior. The food consumption data in Figure 8 showing overconsumption in mutants and rescue by InR blockade are not questioned.

result: The reduced positive reinforcing effect of sucrose at high glycogen levels combined with increased stability of food-related memories due to prolonged starvation could lead to increased food intake and dysregulation. Overconsumption becomes visible after prolonged hunger, correlating with emerging stable LTM. The stability of appetitive memory could trigger food overconsumption. Loss of octopamine regulation could promote dysregulation of food intake.
evaluation: These are speculative claims about broader implications that reviewers do not explicitly evaluate. While reviewers praise the overall study, they do not specifically comment on these speculative connections to food intake dysregulation. Reviewer 1 notes 'The conclusions are well supported by the data' but this refers to the experimental findings, not these speculative extensions. These claims go beyond what was directly tested and represent the authors' interpretation of potential implications.

result: TβhnM18 mutants are not defective in appetitive memory formation per se; rather, internal energy status defines how quickly memories form. Octopamine acts upstream of dopaminergic neurons in LTM formation, controlling gain in memory formation. The internal energy status influences how external sucrose is evaluated rather than octopamine being directly involved in STM acquisition. The octopaminergic system integrates internal energy demands and evaluation of external food supplies, modulating sensory perception of both conditioned stimulus and reward. This allows selective regulation of food-related behaviors.
evaluation: Reviewers support this integrative interpretation. Reviewer 1 states this work 'sheds light on the enduring question of the octopaminergic neuronal system's involvement in appetitive memory formation' and notes the authors 'propose a mechanism' that is well-supported. Reviewer 2 notes the work 'clarified the role of the monoamine Octopamine' and 'provides insight about interconnections between energy levels, feeding and formation of short-term and long-term food-related memories.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'The overall take-home message of the manuscript is clear and supported by the data presented.'

result: The results support a feedback mechanism between glycogen levels in muscles and the brain, with muscles and fat bodies communicating about energy content and signaling this information back to the brain. This feedback remains intact in octopamine-deficient mutants, as TβhnM18 mutants still form STM when energy storage is sufficiently reduced.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation based on the tissue-specific glycogen manipulation experiments. Reviewer 1 notes the 'meticulously designed' experiments and that 'conclusions are well supported by the data.' Reviewer 2 states the authors 'used a range of approaches, performed carefully controlled experiments and produced high quality data.' The logic connecting the requirement for glycogen reduction in both tissues to inter-tissue communication is not challenged.

result: The close relationship between the octopaminergic and noradrenergic neurotransmitter systems suggests that the integrator function may be conserved across species.
evaluation: This speculative claim about evolutionary conservation is not evaluated by reviewers. While reviewers note the work will be 'of interest to the growing community of biologists interested in how internal state shapes behavior' (Editor/Reviewer), they do not specifically comment on whether the mechanism is likely conserved. This represents the authors' speculation about broader implications beyond the Drosophila data presented.
